name: Omi.ai — Onboarding Mentor Intelligence
description: An AI onboarding SaaS, now a working MVP: an employee's recorded, narrated work sessions become a knowledge base per role, and new hires learn with an AI mentor that cites its sources.
context: When someone leaves, their know-how often leaves with them. Omi.ai records how they actually work and turns it into procedures the new hire can question.

I designed and built it end to end: recording and upload, the AI pipeline, the retrieval behind the chat, the onboarding guide, analytics and the marketing site. Omi.ai is incubated at NEOMA Business School.

Status: a working MVP, ready for first user tests. I chose narrated recordings over capturing on-screen actions (Microsoft Clarity's open-source recording technology) because it reached testers sooner, and an AI might well misread a screen nobody explains.

work.title: Why the MVP stays as it is for now
work.text: I don't change a product in a vacuum: once the base works, real use decides what comes next.
points: No new features or redesigns until enough real users have given feedback.
Phase two starts only when that feedback is good enough by my own criteria. Not perfect, good enough.

work.title: Capture and AI-written procedures
work.text: The employee records their screen while explaining it out loud, then uploads the video.
points: The narration is transcribed and a vision model describes key frames.
Omi drafts a step-by-step procedure (SOP); each step cites its narration lines and recording moments.
A coverage score and warnings guide the review. Nothing reaches the AI until a human publishes it.
Each procedure also exports as a PDF.
Phase two: a browser extension capturing on-screen actions automatically, on Clarity's open-source technology.

work.title: A "Brain" per role (RAG)
work.text: Published procedures become a searchable knowledge base per job.
points: One step = one excerpt, embedded in Supabase with pgvector.
OpenAI or Mistral, with a local BM25 fallback when there's no API key.
Each excerpt records its embedding model, so indexes never mix.

work.title: Omi Companion, the AI mentor
work.text: A chat that answers from published procedures only.
points: Every answer cites procedure, step and recording moment.
Below a calibrated relevance threshold it says "I don't know" and suggests who to ask.

work.title: Onboarding guide and Obsidian export
points: A five-module guide per role: the job, its rhythm, procedures in learning order, contacts, edge cases.
Flagged as outdated when a procedure changes; Markdown export.
A full Obsidian vault, with roles, tools and contacts linked in a graph.

work.title: Measured quality
points: Unit tests on masking, procedure generation, chunking and answers.
Demo Brain: 10/10 on known questions, 6/8 on unseen ones, off-topic questions refused.
Per-role analytics: coverage, onboarding velocity, blocking points.

name: Kompute — batch AI jobs on idle gaming GPUs
description: Entrepreneurship class team project: a marketplace running small teams' batch AI jobs on idle gaming PCs. Stopped as a business; it continues only as the class project.
context: It started as a personal project I'd paused: running other people's workloads safely on private PCs needs sandboxing skills I didn't have, and I wouldn't ship something unsafe. The class let our team rethink it as a business: who needs it, what it should cost, what a credible first version looks like. A team effort, not mine alone.
No customers, providers or revenue, and the site says so. The class project started in September 2026 and is still running.

work.title: The idea
work.text: Small AI teams need GPU power for batch work; millions of gaming GPUs sit idle most of the day.
points: Jobs that fit: non-sensitive, interruptible, single-GPU (embeddings, batch inference to classify, tag or summarise, transcription of public audio…).
Gamers keep 85% of what each job pays and choose their hours; games always come first, and the job moves as soon as one starts.
Not a fit: multi-GPU training, real-time serving, personal or confidential data.

work.title: How it works
work.text: Built for PCs that can vanish at any moment.
points: Jobs split into checkpointed chunks.
The gaming PC pulls work over HTTPS; nothing connects into the player's home network.
Heartbeat every 2 s; after 10 s of silence the job resumes on another machine from its last checkpoint.
Random items recomputed before delivery; one ordered result file.
For teams, a cheaper option for work that can wait a few minutes: no cloud GPUs to rent or maintain, and help packaging their first job.

work.title: Business model and what is built
work.text: Pricing tested in interviews, not yet validated by payments: €0.30–0.40 per GPU-hour, 15% commission.
points: A live demo runs a real embeddings job that survives being unplugged (on a CPU server, not a gaming GPU).
A quote form saved to a database, answered by hand.
The marketplace dashboard (providers, wallet, payouts) is a mock-up with demo data.

work.title: Why I stopped Kompute as a business
work.text: The skills and the numbers didn't add up.
points: Security: running strangers' code on someone's PC safely takes years of security and data-flow expertise, learned next to senior engineers. I couldn't get there fast enough.
Economics, the bigger problem: thin margins mean a huge customer base, and winning it would cost more (CAC) than each customer brings.
Still on my mind: computing power and graphics cards are scarce. Maybe another angle one day.

work.title: What the business plan says, honestly
work.text: Written as if we were launching for real:
points: Outside funding required (business angel, Bpifrance or similar).
A co-founder specialised in security and data flows required.
The first acquisition campaign would make or break it.
A class exercise, but real observations and the calls we'd have made.
